sector: Formaldehyde-free protein wood adhesives (soy/gluten plywood, particleboard)
opportunity: Urea-formaldehyde resins emit carcinogenic formaldehyde; enzymatic isopeptide crosslinking of soy/wheat-gluten proteins builds a water-resistant thermoset network, enabling non-toxic, renewable, formaldehyde-free bonding of wood composites.
tg_fit: mTG catalyzes Gln-Lys crosslinks in gluten/soy adhesives; wheat-gluten adhesive combining TG + epichlorohydrin reached ~3.21 MPa dry / 0.81 MPa wet shear, meeting plywood standards. Emerging only: TG alone is insufficient and cheaper chemical crosslinkers (polyamidoamine-epichlorohydrin/PAE, epoxies, pMDI) dominate commercial soy adhesives.
evidence: Wheat-gluten wood adhesive enhanced by transglutaminase plus epichlorohydrin exceeded Chinese plywood shear-strength standards, but PAE remains the dominant commercial soy crosslinker.

sources.title: Properties of wheat gluten based wood adhesives enhanced by transglutaminase and epichlorohydrin
Recent Advances on the Development of Protein-Based Adhesives for Wood Composite Materials—A Review

verification.note: TG+chemical combo demonstrated in peer-reviewed work; TG not commercially dominant vs PAE.

sector: Keratin valorization from waste feathers/wool/hair into films & materials
opportunity: Millions of tonnes of keratin waste (poultry feathers, wool, hair) are landfilled/incinerated; crosslinking recovered keratin into cohesive, water-resistant films/biomaterials adds value and diverts waste.
tg_fit: mTG (transamidation) forms isopeptide crosslinks in low-MW keratin and keratin/PVA blends, improving compactness and mechanical/water resistance; also self-crosslinks keratin on wool. Emerging; frequently benchmarked against cheaper CaCl2 and genipin, which are often competitive or superior.
evidence: Keratin transamidation by mTG and TG-crosslinked feather-keratin/PVA and wool-keratin films are documented, though genipin/CaCl2 are studied side-by-side as low-cost alternatives.

sources.title: Keratin transamidation (microbial transglutaminase)

Transglutaminase-modified wool keratin film and potential application in tissue engineering

verification.note: Multiple independent peer-reviewed studies confirm mTG crosslinking of keratin; competitiveness vs genipin/CaCl2 noted.

opportunity: Wet-strength resins keep paper intact when wet; most are fossil-based polyamidoamine-epichlorohydrin (PAE) that release AOX/chloropropanols. Enzymatic protein/polymer crosslinking promises non-toxic, bio-based wet-strength development.
tg_fit: mTG could crosslink protein sizing/coatings on fibers, but there is little direct evidence of TG in commercial papermaking; bio-based wet-strength research centers on oxidized-cellulose/polyamine systems, and PAE dominates the market. TG here is largely speculative and cost-uncompetitive.
evidence: Sustainable wet-strength research focuses on oxidized hydroxypropyl-cellulose/polyamine crosslinking comparable to fossil PAE; direct mTG use in paper is not established commercially.

sources.title: Cross-Linking of Oxidized Hydroxypropyl Cellulose in Paper: Paper Wet Strength Development
Wet Reinforcing of Paper and Board by Novel Crosslinking Chemicals

verification.note: TG mechanism is plausible for protein-sized paper but no direct commercial/peer evidence; PAE dominates.

opportunity: Regenerated protein fibers (soy, casein, collagen) and protein-finished textiles are renewable alternatives to petro-fibers but are weak and dissolve/felt; crosslinking raises tensile strength, thermal stability, and wash durability.
tg_fit: mTG grafts casein onto wool yarns (higher tensile strength, smoothness) and crosslinks collagen with casein/keratin/soy protein isolate to improve thermal stability and mechanical properties of fiber-forming proteins. Emerging; enzyme cost limits scale-up vs conventional finishing chemistries.
evidence: mTG-catalyzed crosslinking of type I collagen with casein/keratin/soy protein improved thermal stability and mechanics, and casein grafting onto wool improved fiber strength.

sources.title: Improved thermal-stability and mechanical properties of type I collagen by crosslinking with casein, keratin and soy protein isolate using transglutaminase
Enzyme-catalyzed protein crosslinking (review)

verification.note: Peer-reviewed evidence for mTG fiber/textile protein grafting; commercial scale limited.

opportunity: Edible/co-extruded collagen casings replace natural gut with uniform, strong tubing; crosslinking reinforces the collagen matrix (higher burst pressure/tensile strength) so casings survive filling, cooking, and handling.
tg_fit: mTG mediates Gln-Lys amide bonds reinforcing the collagen 3D matrix; TG-modified collagen fibers show improved crosslinking and film properties when denatured >=35 C. Emerging-to-applied for casings; glutaraldehyde and dehydrothermal/physical crosslinking are cheaper incumbents in casing manufacture.
evidence: TG crosslinking significantly raised burst pressure and strengthened collagen gels/fibers, and reviews cite crosslinking as key to co-extruded collagen casing performance.

sources.title: Collagen use for co-extruded sausage casings – A review
Cross-linking and film-forming properties of transglutaminase-modified collagen fibers tailored by denaturation temperature

verification.note: TG collagen reinforcement well supported; specific casing commercialization vs physical crosslinking is mixed.

opportunity: Pea/gluten/hydrocolloid protein bioplastics are renewable and compostable but brittle and water-sensitive; enzymatic crosslinking strengthens the matrix and lowers water uptake for durable molded articles (not packaging).
tg_fit: mTG introduces ε-(γ-glutamyl)lysine bonds in compression-molded pea-protein and hydrocolloid bioplastics, converting α-helix to β-sheet network and strengthening the matrix. Emerging/research; glycerol plasticizing plus cheap crosslinkers (cinnamaldehyde, dialdehydes, citric acid) compete on cost.
evidence: NMR/FTIR confirmed mTG-induced isopeptide bonds and β-sheet enrichment strengthening protein thermoformed bioplastics; hydrocolloid-based bioplastics were similarly improved by mTG.

sources.title: Transglutaminase as an Enzymatic Crosslinker of Protein-Based Thermoformed Bioplastics
Microbial Transglutaminase as a Tool to Improve the Features of Hydrocolloid-Based Bioplastics

verification.note: Two independent peer-reviewed studies; but distinct from excluded packaging films and still lab-scale.

sector: Leather-waste collagen/gelatin valorization into films, adhesives & leather filler
opportunity: Chrome-tanned leather trimmings/shavings are hazardous landfill waste; collagen/gelatin recovered from them can be crosslinked into films, wood adhesives, and re-tanning fillers, closing the loop on tannery waste.
tg_fit: mTG crosslinks recovered gelatin films (higher strength, lower water solubility/permeability) and mediates collagen-casein bonding to upgrade low-quality leather as a filler. Emerging/research; glutaraldehyde and oxidized-sugar crosslinkers are cheaper and studied in parallel.
evidence: TG-crosslinked gelatin films from tanned-leather waste and an enzymatic collagen-casein crosslinking process for leather filler are reported; glutaraldehyde-crosslinked variants are the low-cost comparators.

sources.title: Transglutaminase Crosslinked Gelatin Films Extracted from Tanned Leather Waste (JALCA)
From leather wastes to leather: enhancement of low quality leather using collagen recovered from leather tanned wastes
Recycling of collagen from solid tannery waste and prospective utilization as adhesives

verification.note: Multiple independent peer-reviewed sources on mTG valorization of leather-waste collagen/gelatin.

opportunity: Crosslinking gelatin shells/films tunes dissolution, thermal stability and mechanical integrity for modified-release capsules and industrial gelatin coatings; enzymatic control avoids toxic residual chemical crosslinkers.
tg_fit: mTG achieves >90% gelatin crosslinking under mild aqueous conditions, raising strength and slowing/blocking dissolution (basis for controlled release). Dual role: deliberate engineering opportunity but also mirrors an unwanted capsule cross-linking defect; aldehydes are the classic (undesirable) crosslinker to displace.
evidence: mTG crosslinks gelatin under mild conditions (>90% crosslink) increasing strength and slowing dissolution, while capsule literature shows crosslinking otherwise causes slower/incomplete drug release.

verification.note: mTG gelatin crosslinking well documented; the material/excipient framing is emerging and double-edged.

opportunity: Metal mordants (chrome, tin) in natural dyeing are toxic/effluent-heavy; a protein bio-mordant that grafts extra dye-binding sites onto fibers enables cleaner, higher-color-yield natural dyeing (distinct from anti-shrink finishing).
tg_fit: mTG functionalizes wool surface as a bio-mordant, boosting madder dye uptake and colorfastness (optimum ~5% mTG, 10% alum). Emerging/research; still paired with alum and competes with cheaper conventional mordanting.
evidence: mTG surface functionalization of wool acted as a bio-mordant improving dyeability with madder and washing/rubbing colorfastness.

Surface functionalization of wool via microbial-transglutaminase and bentonite as bio-nano-mordant

verification.note: Two peer-reviewed studies; niche and lab-scale, distinct from excluded wool anti-shrink.

sector: Natural-fiber green composites with crosslinked protein matrix
opportunity: Green composites pair natural fibers (hemp, pulp) with biodegradable protein resins, but protein matrices are water-sensitive and weak; crosslinking the matrix improves load transfer, water resistance and durability for fully compostable composites.
tg_fit: mTG is proposed as a safe green crosslinker for protein matrices in sustainable material research, improving film/matrix cohesion and barrier properties. Largely conceptual for structural composites; cheaper crosslinkers and PLA/PBS biopolymer matrices dominate real green-composite practice.
evidence: Reviews position transglutaminase as a green crosslinker improving protein-matrix mechanical/barrier properties, but structural natural-fiber composite use remains conceptual.

sources.title: Advances in transglutaminase cross-linked protein-based packaging films; a review
Transglutaminase in Future Foods: Applications in Sustainable Protein Systems

verification.note: Crosslinked protein matrices proven for films; structural composite use is extrapolated/conceptual.

opportunity: Casein glues are historic renewable wood adhesives (WWI aircraft plywood) enjoying a formaldehyde-free comeback for veneer and laminated timber; crosslinking boosts water resistance, a classic casein weakness.
tg_fit: mTG can crosslink casein (and casein-collagen) to raise strength/water resistance, extending water-resistant casein adhesive formulations. Emerging for the enzyme angle; commercial water-resistant casein adhesives currently rely on lime/metal-salt and synthetic co-binders rather than TG.
evidence: Water-resistant casein adhesives for veneer bonding are documented and protein-adhesive reviews note enzymatic crosslinking (incl. TG) to enhance casein/collagen glues, though lime-based systems remain standard.

sources.title: Water-Resistant Casein-Based Adhesives for Veneer Bonding in Biodegradable Ski Cores
Recent Advances on Protein-Based Adhesives for Wood Composite Materials—A Review

verification.note: Casein glue marketed; explicit mTG enhancement is emerging, not the commercial norm.

sector: Plant transglutaminase in agronomy (photosynthesis, stress, fertilization)
opportunity: Endogenous plant TGs conjugate polyamines and crosslink cytoskeleton and photosynthetic antenna proteins, influencing pollen-tube growth, photosynthetic efficiency, stress tolerance and senescence — a lever for crop improvement/biostimulation.
tg_fit: This is plant-endogenous TG biology (plastid/pollen TGs), not applied mTG dosing; agronomic exploitation (engineering TG activity or polyamine-TG modules for yield/stress resilience) is a genuine but speculative new angle rather than a marketed input.
evidence: Plant TGs are confirmed widespread crosslinking enzymes with functional roles in photosynthesis (LHCII polyamination), pollen-tube growth and stress responses, but translation to an agronomic product is unproven.

sources.title: Transglutaminases: Widespread Cross-linking Enzymes in Plants
Role of Plastid Transglutaminase in LHCII Polyamination and Thylakoid Electron/Proton Flow
Plant Transglutaminases: New Insights in Biochemistry, Genetics, and Physiology

verification.note: Biology is well established across multiple reviews; the agronomic application remains conceptual.

opportunity: Coated (slow-release) fertilizers cut nutrient leaching and emissions; replacing polyurethane/sulfur shells with biodegradable protein coatings whose permeability is tuned by crosslinking would give compostable controlled-release granules.
tg_fit: mTG could crosslink protein (soy, collagen/leather-protein) coatings to modulate water uptake and nutrient-release rate, but no direct TG-coated CRF evidence exists; the field uses bio-based coatings crosslinked by oxidized sugars, glutaraldehyde or drying, and cheap incumbents dominate. Speculative.
evidence: Reviews of bio-based CRF coatings cite protein materials (e.g., chicken-leather protein) and biopolymer shells, but transglutaminase crosslinking of such coatings is not reported.

sources.title: Optimizing coating materials and processes for controlled-release coated urea: Review of bio-based coating materials
Production, Mechanisms, and Performance of Controlled-Release Fertilizers Encapsulated with Biodegradable-Based Coatings

verification.note: No direct evidence of mTG in CRF coatings; opportunity inferred from protein-coating literature.

sector: Seed coating & priming with crosslinked-protein biostimulant delivery
opportunity: Seed coatings deliver nutrients, biostimulants and microbial inoculants at germination; a crosslinked protein/biopolymer shell could protect payloads, control release and improve adhesion and germination under stress.
tg_fit: mTG could crosslink protein-based seed-coat matrices (analogous to silk/alginate delivery coatings) to tune release and encapsulate inoculants, but no direct TG seed-coating evidence exists; alginate, chitosan and silk are the studied matrices. Speculative.
evidence: Seed-coating delivery systems for bio-based biostimulants and protein-hydrolysate priming are established, but transglutaminase-crosslinked seed coatings are not documented.

sources.title: A Seed Coating Delivery System for Bio-Based Biostimulants to Enhance Plant Growth
Seed Priming With Protein Hydrolysates Improves Arabidopsis Growth and Stress Tolerance

verification.note: TG role is inferred; no direct seed-coating study uses transglutaminase.

opportunity: Polyethylene mulch causes soil 'white pollution'; soy/plant-protein mulch films are soil-biodegradable but too water-sensitive and weak, so crosslinking is needed to extend field service life before controlled degradation.
tg_fit: mTG can crosslink soy/plant-protein films (proven for protein packaging films) to raise strength and lower solubility, applicable to mulch; however, demonstrated soy-protein mulch films use oxidized-sucrose/lignin or citric-acid crosslinkers, which are cheaper than enzyme. Emerging.
evidence: Biodegradable soy-protein mulch films crosslinked with oxidized sucrose/lignin are reported, and mTG is an established protein-film crosslinker, but enzyme use for mulch specifically is not yet shown vs cheap chemical crosslinkers.

Advances in transglutaminase cross-linked protein-based films; a review

verification.note: Protein mulch films and mTG film crosslinking both real; combination for mulch inferred, cheaper crosslinkers dominate.

opportunity: Synthetic polyacrylamide flocculants leave persistent/toxic monomer residues; renewable protein bioflocculants coagulate colloids to reduce turbidity/COD/color, and crosslinking could raise molecular weight for stronger bridging flocculation.
tg_fit: mTG could enlarge/crosslink protein bioflocculants to enhance bridging capacity, but no direct evidence links TG to flocculant performance; plant-seed and microbial protein flocculants are studied without enzymatic crosslinking. Speculative.
evidence: Plant/protein-derived bioflocculants coagulate wastewater colloids effectively, but transglutaminase-mediated crosslinking of flocculants is not reported.

verification.note: Single supporting source on protein flocculants; TG crosslinking is a hypothesis only.

sector: Protein superabsorbent hydrogels for soil water retention
opportunity: Superabsorbent hydrogels cut irrigation needs and improve sandy-soil water/nutrient retention; a biodegradable protein-based hydrogel would avoid acrylamide residues left by conventional synthetic SAPs in farmland.
tg_fit: mTG crosslinks soy/whey proteins into elastic hydrogels (demonstrated with nanoclay reinforcement), giving a biodegradable network that could hold soil water; agricultural deployment is unproven and synthetic/polysaccharide SAPs dominate on cost/absorbency. Speculative.
evidence: mTG crosslinking enhances elastic properties of soy-protein hydrogels, and superabsorbent hydrogels are established for soil water retention, but protein-TG hydrogels for agriculture are not yet demonstrated.

Superabsorbent Polymer Hydrogels for Sustainable Agriculture: A Review

verification.note: mTG protein hydrogels real; soil-SAP application inferred, synthetic SAPs dominate.
